WIDER CONTEXT
- Heirs of Heinrich Rieger, a Viennese dentist and collector deported to Theresienstadt in 1942, claimed Egon Schiele's watercolour "Kauernder weiblicher Akt", owned by the City of Cologne and held by the Museum Ludwig, from 2016 (City of Cologne, 8 February 2021).
- Cologne had argued that Rieger may have sold the work before the Nazi annexation of Austria (The Art Newspaper, Catherine Hickley, 8 February 2021).
- On 8 February 2021 the German government's advisory commission on Nazi-looted art unanimously recommended restitution to Rieger's heirs, finding that most of Rieger's sales "took place after March 1938 as a consequence of the pressures of Nazi persecution" (The Art Newspaper).
- The city said it had stated from the outset that it would follow the commission's decision, and the cultural administration was to put a restitution proposal to the City Council on 23 March 2021 (City of Cologne).
- The museum's director, Yilmaz Dziewior, said: "We are relieved that there are now prospects for a fair and just solution with the return of the work to the family." (The Art Newspaper)

- From 2016 the heirs of Heinrich Rieger, a Viennese dentist and collector deported to Theresienstadt in 1942, claimed Egon Schiele's watercolour "Kauernder weiblicher Akt", owned by the City of Cologne and held by the Museum Ludwig; the city and the heirs agreed to put the case to the German government's advisory commission on Nazi-looted art (City of Cologne, 8 February 2021).
